messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological PTSD case vignettes.
Write in third person as a realistic personal narrative —
the kind a therapist might write after getting to know a patient over several sessions.
The vignette should describe a real person's lived experience,
not a clinical report or a list of symptoms.
Vignettes should be 500–700 words.

Important:
- Tell the story chronologically — from the traumatic event to the present
- Show symptoms through what the patient thinks, feels, and does
- Integrate the patient's occupation naturally into the story
- Do NOT end with a diagnosis or treatment recommendation

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.

Patient demographics:
- Age: 54
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Software Engineer
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 77

Amir presents as a man meticulously put together. His clothes are neat, his posture is rigid, and he speaks in the precise, logical manner of the software engineer he has been for thirty years. He describes his life as a series of well-defined functions and routines, a system he has built to ensure stability. But over the last several months, he says, the system has been failing. There are bugs he cannot fix.

The initial event, the one he refers to as “the incident in Chicago,” happened when he was 28. He was at a tech conference, a rising star at his company. He speaks of that time with a detached nostalgia, remembering the excitement of the industry, the feeling of being on the cusp of something new. On the last night, a senior executive from a partner company, a charismatic and well-respected man, invited him out for drinks to celebrate a potential deal. Amir felt honored. He remembers the warmth of the whiskey, the loud music of the hotel bar, and the man’s hand on his shoulder, which felt paternal at first.

He doesn’t narrate the rest of that night in a linear fashion. The memory comes in fragments, like corrupted data packets. The feeling of being steered not towards the lobby, but to the elevator. The sudden, dizzying sense that he had had far too much to drink. The metallic click of a hotel room door. He recalls staring at the patterned carpet, trying to make sense of the repeating geometric shapes as a way to anchor himself, while his body was being used in a way he couldn't process. There was no overt violence, no struggle he can recall. There was only a profound sense of paralysis and confusion, a complete system override where his own commands were ignored. He woke up alone in the early morning, the room smelling of stale alcohol and an unfamiliar cologne. He showered until the water ran cold, dressed, and took the first flight home, never mentioning it to anyone.

For over two decades, he managed to archive the memory. He poured himself into his work, finding solace in the clean, binary logic of code. In programming, there is always a reason for an error, a solution to be found. His personal life, however, became a fortress of solitude. He told himself he was too dedicated to his career for a serious relationship. Dates were rare and always ended before any real intimacy could develop. A woman’s hand on his arm during dinner would be enough to make him retreat, the touch feeling less like affection and more like an intrusion. He explained his aversion to crowds and loud bars as a simple preference for quiet. He attributed his chronic insomnia and the occasional, jarring nightmares to work stress.

The system began to crash six months ago when his company hired a new senior manager. The man is physically unassuming, but he has the same brand of easy, back-slapping charisma as the executive from Chicago. He wears a similar cologne. The first time the manager clapped Amir on the shoulder in a meeting, Amir felt an electric jolt of panic so intense he almost knocked over his laptop.

Now, his carefully constructed world is riddled with errors. The smell of the cologne drifts down the hallway and Amir’s heart begins to pound, the memory of the hotel room carpet flashing behind his eyes. He finds himself unable to concentrate, staring at lines of code that suddenly seem like a foreign language. He has started working entirely from home, citing productivity, but in truth, it is to avoid the office. His apartment, once a sanctuary, now feels like a prison. He double-checks the locks on his door multiple times before bed. He sleeps in short, fitful bursts, often waking up drenched in sweat, his own choked gasp echoing in the silent room. He feels a constant, simmering anger just beneath his skin, an irritation with the world that he cannot explain or control. He lives in a state of high alert, his mind perpetually running a background process that scans for a threat he can’t see but feels in every cell of his body.
